analysis.one_liner: Imposes duties of care, loyalty, and confidentiality on companies handling people's online data.
analysis.headline: Introduced in December 2025 with 14 Senate cosponsors — all Democrats or independents — the bill sits in the Senate Commerce Committee with no hearing, markup, or vote taken since referral.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would treat the companies that collect your online data like fiduciaries: they would have to secure it, tell you quickly if sensitive data is breached, and could not use or sell it in ways that hurt you. The Federal Trade Commission and state attorneys general would enforce the rules, with penalties that scale by the number of days out of compliance or users harmed. The bill also covers nonprofits and phone and cable companies, which the FTC normally cannot police.
analysis.who_benefits: Everyone who uses the internet. The bill gives legal duties to the platforms, apps, and services that collect data linked to you — including health data, precise location, biometrics, and private messages. It requires them to secure that data, notify you of breaches of sensitive information, and stops them from selling or sharing your data with outside firms unless those firms agree to the same duties and can be audited. State attorneys general could sue violators and collect penalties that grow with the number of users harmed, and the rights could not be signed away in a terms-of-service agreement.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Internet users and their personal data

how_it_helps.text: Requires online service providers to reasonably secure individual identifying data and to promptly inform users of any breach involving their sensitive data, such as health records, precise location, financial account numbers, or biometric identifiers.

Bars providers from using personal data, or data derived from it, in any way that benefits the provider to the user's detriment and causes foreseeable material physical or financial harm, or that would be unexpected and highly offensive to a reasonable user.

Prohibits selling or sharing personal data with anyone else unless that person signs a contract imposing the same duties of care, loyalty, and confidentiality — and the provider audits that person's data practices on a regular basis.

Enforcement runs through the FTC as an unfair or deceptive practice and through state attorneys general, who can win civil penalties calculated per day of noncompliance or per user harmed; the bill extends FTC authority to nonprofits and common carriers, which the FTC Act normally does not cover.
The new rights and remedies cannot be waived or limited by contract, so a click-through terms-of-service agreement cannot strip them away.

analysis.who_pays: Online companies that monetize personal data — advertising-driven platforms, data brokers, and app networks — would bear compliance costs, audit obligations, restrictions on selling or sharing data, and penalty exposure from FTC and state attorney general lawsuits. Some of those costs could reach users through higher prices, more paywalls, or fewer free ad-supported services.

drawbacks.text: Individuals cannot sue on their own; enforcement depends entirely on the FTC and state attorneys general, so a person whose data was misused has no personal day-in-court remedy under this bill.
State civil penalties apply only to providers that 'knowingly or repeatedly' violated the duties, so a first-time careless violator faces FTC remedies but not the per-user state penalty.

The FTC can exempt categories of providers based on their size, complexity, and the costs and benefits of applying the duties, which could leave smaller firms outside the protections while the largest data collectors remain fully covered.

Standards like 'unexpected and highly offensive' and 'detriment' are broad, and the audit and data-segregation obligations would impose real compliance costs; critics would argue those costs get passed to users and that legal uncertainty chills product development.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits are broad and concrete: breach notification for sensitive data, a legal backstop against selling personal data to unchecked third parties, and penalties that scale with the number of people harmed. The main honest criticisms are structural — no private right of action and regulator discretion to exempt small firms — plus genuine compliance costs for data-dependent businesses. On balance this is a consumer-protection bill whose costs fall mostly on companies whose revenue depends on unrestrained data collection, not on the people whose data it is.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Commerce Committee on the day it was introduced and no committee or floor action has been taken since.

narrative.text: Sen. Brian Schatz introduced the Data Care Act of 2025 in the Senate on December 18, 2025.
The bill was read twice and referred to the Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation the same day.
Fourteen senators cosponsored the bill — 12 of the 45 Senate Democrats and both Senate independents (Angus King and Bernie Sanders); no Republican has signed on.
The full action history shows no hearing, markup, committee vote, or floor action after the referral to committee.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: As of now, the online platforms and data brokers that profit from unrestricted collection and resale of personal data are better off: the status quo continues while the bill waits in committee with no scheduled action.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Platforms and data brokers, for now

sides.party_line_note: Every cosponsor is a Democrat or independent (12 of 45 Senate Democrats plus both independents); none of the 55 Senate Republicans has signed on, and the Republican-controlled committee and floor schedule have left the bill untouched since referral.

industries.industry: Advertising-driven online platforms (search, social media, app networks)
industries.note: These companies would have to secure the personal data they collect, notify users of sensitive-data breaches, and stop selling or sharing data with firms that do not take on the same duties — constraints aimed squarely at the behavioral-advertising business model. They keep operating under the law, but their freedom to monetize data against users' interests ends.

industries.industry: Data brokers and data analytics firms
industries.note: The bill bars providers from selling or transferring personal data unless the buyer contracts to the same care, loyalty, and confidentiality duties and submits to regular audits, and state attorneys general can pursue penalties per user harmed. Their resale-and-profiling model depends on data moving without those strings.
The bill expressly extends FTC enforcement to common carriers, closing a long-standing jurisdictional gap that has shielded broadband and wireless providers from FTC privacy policing.
The bill covers nonprofits that collect personal data, which the FTC Act generally does not reach, closing another enforcement gap.
The FTC may exempt providers by size after weighing privacy risk against compliance costs, so the smallest firms may escape the duties — relief for them, but a protection gap for their users.

analysis.trajectory: The bill has no Republican cosponsors, and the Senate Commerce Committee has taken no action in the weeks since referral. The most likely path is that it sits in committee without a hearing or vote until the 119th Congress ends, as prior versions of this proposal have done; movement would require the committee chair to schedule action or a bipartisan cosponsor to change the calculus.
